summary: Solomon Islands is an archipelagic country in the South Pacific made up of nearly a thousand islands; in World War II Guadalcanal was the site of fierce fighting between the United States and Japan, and the country became independent from Britain in 1978.

ranking.name: Anglicanism
ranking.description: The Anglican Melanesian Mission was founded in 1849 by the New Zealand bishop Selwyn, recruiting islanders to be trained in New Zealand and then return home to evangelize. In 1871 Bishop Patteson was killed in the Santa Cruz Islands, and his martyrdom in fact stimulated a surge of missionary enthusiasm. After Britain established a protectorate in 1893, Anglicanism expanded rapidly on the central and eastern islands, the Church of Melanesia became an independent province in 1975, and it remains the largest denomination.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: The Catholic Marist missionaries first arrived in the Solomon Islands in 1845, but failed at first because of disease and conflict. After 1898 the Marists re-entered and established mission stations and schools in places such as Guadalcanal and Malaita, and Catholicism thus became the second largest denomination.

ranking.name: South Sea Evangelical Church
ranking.description: The South Sea Evangelical Church grew out of the 'Queensland Kanaka Mission' founded in 1882 on the sugar plantations of Queensland, Australia, for recruited islander laborers, who after returning home established churches on Malaita. It was renamed the South Sea Evangelical Church in 1964 and is concentrated mainly on Malaita.

ranking.name: Seventh-day Adventist Church
ranking.description: The Seventh-day Adventist Church arrived in 1914 and evangelized in the New Georgia Islands of Western Province, attracting followers through schools and hospitals, with some villages converting en masse. The Adventists are especially influential in Western Province.

ranking.name: United Church
ranking.description: The United Church grew out of the Australian Methodist mission that entered Western Province in 1902, and in 1968 merged with other churches to become the United Church. It is concentrated mainly in Western Province, and together with the Adventists forms the two major denominations of the west.

religion.background: The indigenous people of the Solomon Islands believed in ancestral spirits and deities, and the practice of venerating ancestors' skulls was once very widespread. From 1849 the Anglican, Catholic and other missions entered in succession, and in the late 19th and early 20th centuries large numbers of islanders converted to Christianity. The various missions worked on different islands, producing a distribution in which each island is dominated by a particular denomination. During World War II the Guadalcanal campaign took place here. After independence in 1978 Christians have made up more than ninety percent of the population, and the churches play an important role in society and politics.

ranking.name: Solomon Islands Pijin
ranking.description: Solomon Islands Pijin is an English-based creole that arose from the common language among islander laborers recruited in the 19th century to work on the sugar plantations of Queensland, Australia, and Fiji. Because the Solomon Islands have more than seventy languages, after the laborers returned home Pijin became the common language among the inhabitants of different islands, and today most people can use it, with young people in cities such as Honiara speaking it as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English became the language of administration and education during the British protectorate of 1893–1978 and, after independence in 1978, is the sole official language, used in government, law and school education. However, only about 2% speak English as a mother tongue, mainly elite families in the cities, and most people use Pijin and local languages in daily life.

language.history: The Solomon Islands have more than seventy languages, most of them belonging to the Austronesian family and a few to the Papuan families. In the 19th century missionaries recorded the local languages in the Latin alphabet and translated the Bible. In the late 19th century islanders were recruited to work on the sugar plantations of Queensland and Fiji, giving rise to an English-based Pijin. Britain established a protectorate in 1893, and English became the language of administration. After independence in 1978 English is the official language, and Pijin is the de facto national lingua franca.

ranking.name: Earth oven cooking
ranking.description: A pit is dug in the ground and heated stones are placed in it; taro, sweet potato, pork and fish wrapped in banana leaves are placed on the stones, then covered with leaves and earth and slow-cooked for several hours.
ranking.history: Earth oven cooking is a traditional cooking method shared across the Pacific islands, brought thousands of years ago by Austronesian navigators. In the Solomon Islands, pigs are a symbol of wealth and status and play an important role in bride-price at weddings, reconciliation ceremonies and festivals. The earth oven is usually made after church activities on Sundays and for weddings and important community gatherings, and requires the whole village to cooperate in preparing it.

ranking.name: Taro
ranking.description: Taro is boiled or roasted, or mashed and mixed with coconut milk, wrapped in leaves and baked into a pudding, with a creamy texture and a faint sweetness, often eaten with fish or pork.
ranking.history: Taro is one of the most important traditional staples of the Solomon Islands, brought thousands of years ago by the Austronesians. On many islands the planting and harvesting of taro patches is accompanied by traditional rituals, and taro is also an important item at weddings and for gift exchange. In recent years, with the spread of imported white rice and flour, consumption of taro has declined, but it remains indispensable at traditional gatherings.

ranking.name: Ngali nut (Canarium nut)
ranking.description: The ngali nut is the nut of a tree of the genus Canarium in the Burseraceae family; it has a hard shell, and the kernel inside can be eaten raw, roasted, or added to taro pudding, with a crunchy, oily texture.
ranking.history: The ngali nut has been an important food in the Solomon Islands for thousands of years, and archaeologists have found nut shells thousands of years old at sites on the islands, proving that ancient islanders were already eating it. It is rich in oil and protein and can be stored for a long time, making it an important provision on traditional voyages. In recent years the Solomon Islands have tried to develop it as an export product.

ranking.name: Sweet potato
ranking.description: Sweet potatoes are boiled or roasted in a fire, with a sweet, fluffy texture; they are one of the everyday household staples and are often eaten with coconut milk or fish.
ranking.history: The sweet potato originated in the Americas and reached Melanesia a few hundred years ago through exchange across the Pacific. Because it is drought-tolerant and fast-growing, and especially suited to planting in hilly areas, it has become one of the most common crops in Solomon Islands household gardens. After cyclones or droughts, the sweet potato is often the crop that restores the food supply fastest, which is very important for the islanders' food security.

ranking.name: Cassava pudding
ranking.description: Cassava is grated into a paste, mixed with coconut milk, wrapped in banana leaves and cooked in an earth oven, with a soft, chewy texture and a coconut aroma, and can be cut into pieces to share.
ranking.history: Cassava originated in South America and was widely planted in the Solomon Islands only in the 20th century, because it tolerates poor soil and gives high yields. Cassava pudding combines the traditional coconut milk with earth oven cooking techniques, is a common sweet at Solomon Islands festivals, church events and family gatherings, and is also often sold in markets.
